title: Assessment of the Equivalent Level of Safety Requirements for Small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
relevance: The thesis documents actual manual landing tests with Great Planes Giant BigStik aircraft. It identifies the 2010 electric test aircraft as an 80-inch, nominal 13–15 lb Giant BigStik and documents a separate 2013 campaign with newly built electric GBS#10 and GBS#11 aircraft. The 2013 results include per-landing touchdown location and centerline-deviation measurements for RC, fixed-view FPV, and VR control modes.
limitations: This is pilot/control and landing-performance evidence, not an instrumented flight-dynamics identification or model-validation study. The 2010 and 2013 aircraft were not the same physical airframe; the original 2010 model was lost in 2011. The 2013 table contains 12 morning trials, including two rookie-VR attempts recorded as did-not-complete, and four afternoon demonstration runs under worsening weather. No raw telemetry or video files are attached to the thesis.
access: Downloaded from the public Memorial University Scholaris repository. The thesis PDF is unencrypted. The repository does not state a reuse license.
license: No reuse license stated in the repository; copyright notice is retained in the thesis.
read_depth: Selected full text inspected: landing-experiment methods, both 2010 and 2013 test descriptions, trial tables and conclusions, plus GiantStik specifications appendix.

title: Assessment of Alternative Manual Control Methods for Small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
relevance: The peer-reviewed Procedia Manufacturing paper reports the 2013 manual-control landing experiment on a Great Planes GiantStik tail number 10 (GBS#10), comparing unaided RC, fixed-view FPV, and immersive VR approaches. It reports touchdown and runway-centerline measures and qualitative pilot-performance observations.
limitations: This paper substantially overlaps the 2013 campaign reported in Stevenson’s 2015 doctoral thesis and must not be counted as an independent flight campaign. It is not a flight-dynamics identification study and provides no raw flight telemetry. The publisher landing page identified the article as open access, but a direct publisher full-text request returned HTTP 403; only metadata and selected index-visible text were inspected.
access: Metadata verified on the publisher’s ScienceDirect record; publisher record marks the article open access under a Creative Commons license. Direct full-text retrieval returned HTTP 403, so no local original was retained.
license: Publisher record indicates Creative Commons open access; an author-uploaded text identifies CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
read_depth: Publisher metadata and selected search-indexed full-text passages reviewed; the overlapping 2013 methods and results were checked in the corresponding 2015 Stevenson thesis.

title: Aircraft Manoeuvring for Sensor Aiming
relevance: This thesis presents a distinct 2017 instrumented flight campaign on a Great Planes Giant Big Stik UAV. A 25 September 2017 manual open-loop flight used approximately 400 m circuits at 100 m altitude, steady throttle near 25 m/s, and oscillatory aileron, elevator, and rudder inputs to collect identification and validation data. The physical test configuration is specified as electric, 2 m span by 1.4 m length, and approximately 14 kg maximum takeoff weight including 4.5 kg additional payload capacity (the thesis does not report the test-flight mass); it used a 2700 W motor, Pixhawk autopilot, GPS/compass, 915 MHz telemetry, 2.4 GHz RC input, and an independently logging ADIS16488 IMU. The thesis reports fitted rotational/lift models and later attitude-controller and path-following flight demonstrations.
limitations: The identified model is fit for a fixed forward speed of 25 m/s and uses selected conventional manoeuvres, not a broad aerobatic envelope. The thesis presents plotted flight traces, fit statistics, and path-error tables but the public repository record contains no separate raw-log bundle. Its electric setup differs from the piston-powered Giant Big Stik configuration documented in the already-held Cereceda thesis; physical-airframe identity between these campaigns is not established.
access: Downloaded through the public Memorial University Scholaris record. The thesis PDF is unencrypted. The repository does not state a reuse license.
license: No reuse license stated in the repository; the thesis includes its author copyright notice.
read_depth: Full 101-page thesis text inspected, with close review of the aircraft configuration, system-identification method and fits, flight-test table, open-loop manoeuvres, controller tuning, and path-following results.

relevance: The peer-reviewed IEEE SMC conference paper is an exact-model simulation study: its official UWS abstract identifies a Giant Big Stik R/C UAV and describes a JSBSim validation process compared with MATLAB/Simulink AeroSim Blockset. title: My 50-Year Adventure With a Jensen Ugly Stik
relevance: The author reports building his first Jensen Stik in 1974, using it as a spring first-flight model for 51 seasons, and accumulating hundreds of flights while cycling many engines, radios, receivers and servos through it. He says hotter pattern engines increased vertical climb and loop size but did not make level flight faster. The retrospective also records a variable-pitch propeller blade failure that shook off the tail, followed by rebuilding and later conversion to tailwheel gear for a grass field.
limitations: First-person retrospective of one original and a later replacement build. The speed comparison is an unaided observation, not a measured terminal-speed result. No airspeed, flight-time, ready-to-fly weight, CG or control-throw measurements are reported; the article distinguishes the 1974 aircraft from the newer build.

title: RCM Product Review: Great Planes Big Stik 60
relevance: The scan reports a 67.5-inch span, 930-in² wing, 7 lb 12 oz ready-to-fly weight and 19.2 oz/ft² wing loading. The tested example used a Super Tigre G60 FI ABC, Kraft KP7C Series 80 radio and 14 oz tank. The review says the model was balanced at the midpoint of the plan's CG range and control travel was set to the maker's limits; it reports no trim correction, easy loops and rolls, little down-elevator inverted, crisp snaps with recovery by releasing controls, and easy main-wheel landings. It also reports bouncy taxi from low nosewheel loading, improved by reversing the main gear.
limitations: The two-page surviving scan does not name the reviewer or give numeric CG limits or control throws. The weight and wing loading are publication-reported for this single Great Planes 60-size kit installation; the handling comments are qualitative and not instrumented flight data. This 67.5-inch Big Stik is a different variant from the Jensen Ugly Stik 60.
